The season guide

Plot fees for the new season are due by the end of the first month. The waiting list is open.

This guide collects what members have learned over twelve seasons on the river terrace: when to sow, how to keep the soil alive, how we share water and tools, and how a new member gets from an empty plot to a first harvest. It is written by members for members, and it changes every year as we learn more.

1. Before you sow

The terrace soil is heavy clay over river gravel. It holds water well in spring and cracks in late summer. Every plot gets two barrow loads of compost from the shared heaps at the start of the season; dig it into the top spade depth rather than leaving it on the surface, where the blackbirds will scatter it within a week.

Test the soil before you plant anything hungry. The tool shed has a simple kit that reads acidity and the main nutrients in about twenty minutes. Most plots read slightly acidic, which suits potatoes and berries but not brassicas; a handful of garden lime per square metre, worked in a month before planting, fixes that.

  • Clear perennial weeds by hand: bindweed and couch grass regrow from every broken root.
  • Mark paths before you dig, and keep them at least forty centimetres wide for the barrows.
  • Leave the plot edges free for the shared irrigation hose.

2. When to sow

The terrace sits in a frost pocket. Last frosts come about two weeks later here than in the town gardens up the hill, so the dates below are later than the ones printed on seed packets.

CropSow under coverPlant outHarvest
Broad beanslate winterearly springearly summer
Potatoes(chit indoors)mid springmid to late summer
Tomatoesearly springlate springlate summer to autumn
Courgettesmid springearly summersummer
Leeksearly springearly summerautumn to winter
Garlic(direct)autumnearly summer

If a cold night is forecast after you plant out, the shed has fleece on a roll: take what you need and write it in the book by the door so it can be reordered.

3. Water

We share one mains connection and two rainwater tanks. In dry spells the rota on the shed door applies: even-numbered plots water on even dates, odd-numbered plots on odd dates, and nobody uses the hose between eleven in the morning and four in the afternoon. Water the soil, not the leaves, and water deeply twice a week rather than lightly every day; shallow watering keeps roots near the surface, where they dry out first.

Rota, dry spells only
  even plots: even dates   odd plots: odd dates
  no hose 11:00-16:00      tanks first, mains second

4. Compost and soil life

The three heaps behind the shed work in turn: one being filled, one resting, one ready. Put in green waste, shredded paper and the straw from the paths; keep out cooked food, diseased plants and the roots of perennial weeds. Turn the resting heap once a month. A heap that smells is too wet or too green: add straw and turn it.

Mulch bare soil between crops with grass clippings or leaf mould. The worms pull it down over the winter, and in spring the soil crumbles in your hand instead of setting like a brick.

5. Tools and the shed

Tools are shared. Sign them out in the book, clean them before you put them back, and report anything broken so the volunteers can fix it on the first Saturday of the month. Sharp tools hang on the right-hand wall, out of reach of the children's corner.

  1. Spades, forks and rakes: back on their hooks, blades clean.
  2. Hoses: drained and coiled, never left on the paths.
  3. Wheelbarrows: tipped up against the north wall so they do not fill with rain.

6. Your first season

New members get a half plot and a mentor for the first year. Start with crops that forgive mistakes: potatoes, beans, courgettes and salad leaves. Keep a notebook of what you sowed and when; it is the most useful tool in the shed, and next spring you will be glad of it. Come to the work mornings: most of what is in this guide was learned at one of them.

Questions go to the plot secretary through the contact page, or to whoever is in the shed on a Saturday.
